# 09-karsa — sources

Back-test entry `09-karsa.yaml`: Karsa, buying and saving dollar stablecoins where the local currency inflates
(YC Winter 2025). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Karsa (YC W25), 2025-01-30, 215 comments — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42879661 (a comment is cited by its own item URL)
- [LYC] Launch YC: Karsa, the global dollar account — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MgV-karsa-the-global-dollar-account
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/karsa (now "a stablecoin neobank")
- [DAWN23] Dawn, on digital currencies in Pakistan as "a high-tech replacement for hawala-hundi" (headline shortened here), 2023-10-30 — https://www.dawn.com/news/1784968
- [AAJ] Aaj News, "Dollars disappear from open market due to hoarding", 2022-12-15 — https://english.aaj.tv/news/30306930
- [DAWN21] Dawn, "Biometric proof must for buying $500 or above: SBP", 2021-10 — https://www.dawn.com/news/1650577/biometric-proof-must-for-buying-500-or-above-sbp
- [NAYA] NayaPay help, the SBP's annual card limit — https://help.nayapay.com/article/242-what-is-the-annual-card-based-international-transactions-limit-set-by-the-sbp
- [ARAB] Arab News, "Pakistan says has no plans to freeze foreign currency accounts", 2023-06-12 — https://www.arabnews.pk/pakistan/pakistan-says-has-no-plans-to-freeze-foreign-currency-accounts-2320266

## Market

The public material supports **Pakistan** best: the founder's family ([HN] "his uncle in Pakistan"; [LYC] "Shahryar's
family in Pakistan still acutely faces this problem"), the first live sellers ([YCP] "Pakistan, India, Nigeria,
Kenya, Paraguay"), the PKR page discussed in the thread, and the most press on the problem. The segment and all twenty
respondents are in Pakistan. The eval's loader (`instructions/corpus.py`, `MARKET_CURRENCY`) knows only GB, US, IE, FR,
DE, IN, CA and AU, so per the brief the `market` line is **US** (`language: en-US`) and every money value is in USD.
Dollars are also the unit these savers think and buy in (the fee is 1% of the dollars bought). keel-cloud's own
`Market` table does not know PK either, though `Market.chosen` would take PK with an explicit currency.

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** People in Pakistan who earn in rupees and save.
   [HN] "when Shahryar tried explaining [it] to his uncle in Pakistan, it was all jargon until he explained
   stablecoins, which immediately clicked." → `roles[saver]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Keep savings from losing value.
   [HN] "buy and save in stablecoins to protect against currency instability and inflation"; "Over a billion people
   live in countries with severe inflation and are unable to protect their wealth due to strict capital controls."
   → `context.job`, `statements.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When they have rupees left over and want dollars, with the bank and the exchange companies in the
   way. [HN] "earning in a currency thatʼs inflating 20-30% year-over-year"; "good luck getting a foreign currency
   account." [AAJ] dollars "not being readily available in the open market". [DAWN21] exchange companies must "conduct
   biometric verification for all foreign currency sale transactions equivalent to $500 and above". [NAYA] card-based
   international transactions "of up to USD 30,000 per year", "per individual, not per card".
   → `context.circumstance`. Author's choice: the occasion "payday", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out
   of 3, and Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most"): no public figure says how often.

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** [HN] "(1) earning in a currency thatʼs inflating 20-30% year-over-year, (2)
   whoʼs structurally limited from dollar access, and (3) makes payments abroad regularly". → `context.segment`
   (narrowed to Pakistan, the market chosen; condition 3 becomes the Importance rival "Paying for things abroad").

5. **Who pays.** The saver, alone. [HN] "We currently take a 1% transaction fee". → `persona.decision_maker:
   same_person`, Buyer and payer "Nobody else". Author's choice: no other role is named.

6. **Mechanism.** [HN] "Karsa looks and feels like a bank/currency exchange to an average user—they choose an amount
   and buy dollar-denominated stablecoins at a market price. But under the hood, we route our supply from a network of
   verified peer-to-peer stablecoin traders"; "A seller sets their price and deposits money in an escrow smart
   contract"; the buyer "has to send a fiat payment (e.g., bank transfer, payment app, etc.) to the sellerʼs local
   account + upload a photo for verification"; "we ... release the escrowed stablecoins to a digital wallet weʼve
   created for the buyer." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, the Compatibility and Adoption friction items
   (the ID card and payment photo item comes from the same step and from [HN] "we do KYC"). Commitment's step "buy a
   small first amount of dollars" is the author's.

7. **Price.** [HN] "We currently take a 1% transaction fee, though we eventually intend to adjust it proportionally to
   regional FX rates." → `commercial.price` {1, 3, month}: author's arithmetic, 1% of about $100 to $300 of dollars
   bought a month (the amount is the author's choice). Existing sacrifice {5, 15, month}: the premium paid today,
   from [DAWN23] (the PKR-to-USDT premium over the official rate reportedly widened from Rs5-6 to Rs8-9) and [HN] (India:
   "the bid-ask spreads are calamitous - to the tune of 5-6% per side" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42885086),
   taken as 3% to 5% of the same $100 to $300 (author's arithmetic). Ability to pay is derived by code (7% to 60%).

8. **Occasions.** [HN] "Users in these countries already use exchanges like Binance almost like a dollar checking
   account" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42880301 ; a user in Bolivia: "there’s a limit of 50 USD on USD
   transactions per week for each bank" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42881375 (outside the chosen market, so
   it shaped the statement, not a respondent); [DAWN23] "A need for wealth preservation in the face of high inflation and
   currency devaluation"; "a high share of activity happening in Pakistan is through peer-to-peer exchanges".

- Sadia Awan → author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped (rather_not_say) story; money is private.
- Waqas Mirza → author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Nasreen Bibi → gate No: nothing left over to save, after "They need food and water" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42884419

No respondent carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Open
- Market: the loader knows no PK currency, so the entry is US / en-US with dollars while the segment and every
  respondent are in Pakistan. A Keel study in Pakistan would ask in English or Urdu and might price in rupees; that is
  not tested here.
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds (most had it, most say getting
  savings into dollars is one of their two, today's ways fall short); the solution splits on paying a seller they have
  never met (eight of thirteen would); the commercial side splits on what the problem costs them today (several pay
  little or nothing besides inflation) and on taking a first step, while the 1% fee itself holds. This is the author's
  reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- Two respondents transpose accounts from India (the KYC wall, the spread) to Pakistan; the Bolivian $50-a-week limit
  shaped the founder's statement only.
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are three months' worth.
- DAWN23's headline is shortened in the source list: its first word holds a string banned from these files.
- The amount bought a month ($100 to $300), the occasion "payday", the window and the Prevalence bin are the author's.

whys.g1: Both answers are about refusing to hand money to an unknown person online, so one group named plainly 'Won't send money to a stranger' is exactly how I'd sort them.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on this line, so nothing needed keeping out.

insights.line: What would have made a difference?

whys.g1: With only two answers and no groups formed, leaving each on its own is fair: one is about staying safe after being cheated by a P2P seller, the other about already having a dollar account. They share a worry about rising bills, but neither was misplaced or given a vague name.
whys.g2: There is no junk or explicit answer on this line, and both answers drift toward bills rather than what would have helped. Neither was put into a group as if it answered the question.

founder.order_why: The sequence from context to problem to solution to launch reads naturally, but 'How should savers answer?' and 'Who gets a link?' sit under an 'INTERVIEWS · SENT' kicker, so I'm choosing answer mode and recipients after being told the study has gone out, when they belong in step 4 before sending.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 ask the same question, 'Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.', with the recency question between them; if screen 5 is only confirming the context, it should be labelled as a check rather than asked again.
founder.missing: Nothing asked about money: my 1% fee per dollar bought, what savers pay today in exchange-company and P2P premiums, or who pays (the saver alone). There was also no way to name Pakistan as the market or to choose rupees and Urdu, so I sold 'first' in the US even though every saver is in Pakistan. And there was no question about trust in paying a stranger through escrow, which is the step my idea most depends on.

PRIMARY.order_why: Screen 4 asks me to think of my last exchange, but nothing in Part 1 ever asked whether I actually changed rupees into dollars or how, so it jumps in assuming a step that was never set up.
PRIMARY.missing: Whether and how I actually bought dollars in the last 3 months (open market, a dealer, Binance P2P), what premium over the bank rate I paid, and how much hassle it was, like chatting back and forth with each seller to confirm details before every trade.

screens.why1: Straight after I said what it does better than today's way, Keel shows me the benefits it drew from that, which is the obvious next check.
screens.why2: "Dollars at a fair price" and "savings that keep their value" are how my uncle would say it, though "their last exchange" would read better as "the last time they bought dollars".
screens.why3: A Pakistani saver knows what they paid the last time they bought dollars, and whether it was a fair rate, from their own payday purchase.
screens.why4: "Savings that keep their value" is the job itself and any dollars already do that, so it is not better than a dealer's dollars; the real advantage is missing: getting dollars at all without a dealer, a bank account or the $500 ID check.
screens.why5: Fair price is mine, the 1% fee against a 5-6% spread, but the access I pitched has drifted out: buying with a bank transfer and no foreign currency account, the seller's coins held in escrow.
screens.instead: Rows: "Dollars at a fair price" · "Dollars whenever you want, no dealer" · "No foreign currency account needed" · "Seller's dollars held until you pay"; test: "For most, the last time they bought dollars would have gone better with it: dollars at a fair price."

screens.why1: After asking how it fits today's routine and what it does better, asking what a saver must do to start (the KYC and the first peer-to-peer payment) is the obvious next question for a P2P stablecoin product.
screens.why2: 'Setup, extra steps or learning' is plain to me as a fintech founder, and the 25-word limit is clear.
screens.why3: I know the onboarding exactly: we do KYC, the buyer sends a bank or app transfer to a seller's local account, then uploads a photo of the payment.
screens.why4: There is a free-text box plus the single escape 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a founder who doesn't want to test friction.
screens.why5: The belief Keel shows ('Most would pay a verified seller they have never met') keeps my first step but drops the ID card and payment-photo upload I typed, which is half the friction for a saver in Pakistan.
screens.instead: Keep the question; make the belief hold both steps: 'Most would upload their ID card and pay a verified seller they have never met, then send a photo of the payment.'

screens.why1: Right after I said what they must do to start, Keel shows my steps back as a list to check, which is the obvious next screen.
screens.why2: Paying a seller, uploading an ID card and a photo of the payment, and a wallet are all plain to a saver in Pakistan who has bought dollars or USDT before.
screens.why3: Each step is something the saver does or refuses to do themselves when they turn rupees into dollars.
screens.why4: The first two rows are my steps, but 'Set up a wallet in their own name' is off: Karsa creates the wallet for the buyer, so it is not a step they take, and it overlaps the KYC upload.
screens.why5: The seller and ID rows keep what I typed, but the wallet row drifts from my mechanism, where we make the wallet and release the escrowed dollars into it.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Send rupees to a verified seller they've never met' / 'Upload their ID card and a photo of the payment' / 'Buy a small first amount of dollars'; test the first.

screens.why1: Right after Keel wrote the three things a saver must do to start, it makes sense to ask which one I fear most, since only one goes to strangers.
screens.why2: Paying a verified seller, uploading the ID card and payment photo, and the wallet are my own product's steps in my own words, and the question reads on first pass.
screens.why3: I watch exactly where buyers drop off in the P2P flow, so which step scares a rupee saver most is something I know from my own funnel.
screens.why4: The three steps are distinct and the true answer, paying a stranger, is there, but 'set up a wallet in their own name' is slightly off because we create the wallet for the buyer under the hood, so it is not really a step they do.
screens.why5: The belief 'Most would pay a verified seller they have never met' is exactly the trust leap I described: send a bank transfer to a seller's local account against escrow.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? Pay a verified seller they have never met / Upload an ID card and a photo of the payment / Wait for the dollars to be released after paying

screens.why1: After describing the solution and before strangers see the study, asking whether to collect emails from savers who would try a dollar account for real is the natural last step.
screens.why2: Pilot and leave your email are plain to a YC founder, and the hint shows exactly the line respondents will see.
screens.why3: Whether I want early users to sign up for Karsa is my own call, and I'd take a waitlist of Pakistani savers gladly.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two are distinct, and nothing is missing for a binary choice.
screens.why5: The respondent line "Would you try this for real?" leaks nothing, but "pilot" drifts a little from what I'd offer: early access to buy dollars, not a trial program.
screens.instead: Offer early access? People who say yes see: "Would you like to be among the first to try this? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No

screens.why1: Picking who asks my questions is an obvious last step before the link goes out to savers, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: The question, the two voices with 5-second samples, the one-off 400-credit cost and the text-message link all read plainly on the first pass to a founder setting up a study.
screens.why3: I know my respondents, people in Pakistan who earn in rupees and would hear this on their phones, so I can judge which voice they would trust.
screens.why4: The two options are distinct, but both are Western-sounding voices with nothing nearer an accent my Pakistani savers would trust about their money, so the answer I'd want is missing.
screens.why5: It keeps my word 'savers' and leaks nothing of Karsa, the escrow or the sellers to the respondent.
screens.instead: Who should ask savers your questions? ▶ Daphne · ▶ Saskia · ▶ a South Asian English voice (hear each, 5 s; 400 credits whichever you choose)

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the savers, it's natural to choose how they'll answer before the link goes out.
screens.why2: The choice is clear, but the doubled "Daphne Daphne" and the "9 in 10 where it is loud" line need a second read to see that they're about speech recognition.
screens.why3: I know my savers: they're on phones, often in noisy shared homes, and wary of talking about money on video, so I can choose from what I know.
screens.why4: AI voice, read-and-tap, or let them pick covers the real choices, and each is distinct with its readiness shown.
screens.why5: It still says "savers" as I typed, and nothing of Karsa, stablecoins or the seller network leaks into the choice.
screens.instead: How should savers answer? — Read and tap on their phone (ready now) · Talk to Daphne, our AI interviewer, on video (ready in a few minutes) · Let them pick when they open the link

screens.why1: After choosing how savers answer, deciding who gets the link is the natural last step before sending the study out.
screens.why2: The three choices are clear, but 'the Contacts page' is Keel's own term rather than mine, and the label and its description run together ('by name I send each one') so I had to read it twice.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching savers I know by name, like my uncle's circle, or posting in a WhatsApp or Facebook group where Pakistani savers already gather.
screens.why4: Named people, a list found in Keel, and one open link posted to a group are distinct and cover how I would actually reach savers; my pick, people I know by name, is there.
screens.why5: The screen only asks how to reach people, so nothing about Karsa, stablecoins or the saver role is changed or shown to respondents.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (each gets their own link) / A list I find in Keel's contact search (Keel makes a link per person, I send them) / A group I'm already in, like a WhatsApp group (one open link; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits right beside the deciding number, 'Adoption friction: 3 of 7 would do it', so I know at once which belief sank the stage and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows what was counted, over how many and where the bar sits, for example '3 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 2 short', which reads on first look.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names and belief lines are word for word the ones I checked, though the solution statement above them is garbled ('the saver in an app ... the saver chooses', and the wallet clause is said twice).
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next: there is no line saying that trust in paying a stranger is the gap to fix, for example by leading with escrow or verified sellers before the rest; 'What it measures' only explains the method.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible on every card and nothing is called strong, but the page never says seven is a small sample, and Relative advantage is labelled 'Holding up' while sitting exactly at the bar.
screens.instead: Did not hold: only 3 of 7 (one on a condition) would pay a seller they have never met, 2 short of the bar, so trust is the problem to solve next (lead with the escrow and verified sellers); paying by bank transfer and a better price both held, but 7 answers is a small sample and the price advantage only just reached the bar.

screens.why_b1: The status word 'Holding up' sits right beside the deciding number, 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The chart plainly counts answers to 'could you have paid by bank transfer' over 7 people, with the bar marked at 5 and the strip showing 6 for and 1 against.
screens.why_b3: The title Compatibility and 'For most savers, they could pay a seller by bank transfer' are exactly the belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me concretely that bank transfer is not the blocker and points me at adoption friction, the belief that did not hold, as where to work next.
screens.why_b5: The count line keeps n visible and says 'a lean, not a call', but the So line's flat 'is not what will stop them' is firmer than 7 people allow, especially with Imran's cash-in-the-cupboard answer showing cash savers may be stopped exactly here.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 could have paid by bank transfer, a lean, not a call; the one who couldn't keeps savings as cash at home, so cash savers may need another way in. The bigger blocker is adoption friction, below.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "5 of 7 said it would have gone better" against a bar of 5 of 7, marked "at the bar", so I know it held and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The count over 7 and the bar at 5 are plain, but "Better · 5 5 a lot · 0 a little" runs the total and the split together, and I had to read it twice.
screens.why_b3: The title and the line are the ones I checked: Relative advantage, the last exchange going better, dollars at a fair price.
screens.why_b4: The So line sends me on to Adoption friction but doesn't say that clearing the bar with nothing spare means the fair price wins people over only if trust in the seller holds.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, it is called "a lean, not a call", it is flagged as hypothetical, and a pass exactly at the bar is not called strong.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "3 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 2 short", so I know the verdict and the number that decided it at once.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers to the never-met-seller question over 7 people, and the strip shows 3 for, 4 against and the marker at 5, so I don't need a second look.
screens.why_b3: "Most would pay a verified seller they have never met" is the exact line I checked, under the Adoption friction name I saw on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count and says "their reasons are below", but just two of the four quotes appear, and it never says what to change, such as making the escrow and a receipt visible the way the exchange counter is.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays on screen, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" keeps the miss from being read as a final ruling, although "past your bar of 2" briefly mixes the against-count with the 5-of-7 bar.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 won't send rupees to a stranger: they want a counter and a receipt, and the family has a say. Show them the escrow and a receipt before the payment, then ask again.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on its verdict (Did not hold / Holding up) with the deciding count and bar beside it, e.g. 3 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 2 short, and 5 of 7 at the bar for Relative advantage.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and the three belief lines are exactly the ones I checked on the way in, word for word.
screens.why_b4: Beyond the 'When a line fails' heading, nothing says what the failed trust line means for Karsa, such as whether escrow, a receipt or a face at a counter would move the 4 who said no.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, but Adoption friction's count line doesn't add up: 4 against, 2 asked here and 3 named as never seeing it makes 5, so I can't tell who the four are.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me things I didn't type: the counter-and-receipt is what the exchange company really sells, a father's veto over household money, savings held as cash in a cupboard with no bank to transfer from, and that a burned P2P user wants safety over price.
screens.instead: Say the 4 against are Usman, Sana and two others, and that what they would need is a counter and a receipt, someone accountable, before they'd pay a seller they've never met.

screens.why1: As the opening gate it is obvious why it is asked: the study is about people like me who earn in rupees and try to keep savings in dollars.
screens.why2: Earning in rupees is how I'd say it myself; there is nothing to read twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly what currency my salary comes in, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it for a gate, though someone who freelances and gets part of their pay in dollars might pause.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks, but the founder's segment also says no foreign currency account, and this screen only checks the rupee income, so it lets in people the founder meant to leave out.
screens.why6: It is one short question and two options, easy to hear once and answer, though 'Yes or no' alone would say more naturally than 'I'll read 2 options'.
screens.instead: Do you earn in rupees? Yes or no. Then a second gate: Do you have a bank account in dollars? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After asking if I earn in rupees, a check on my savings makes sense, but the story it leads into is about my last exchange, and this question never asks whether I changed rupees to dollars at all.
screens.why2: I understand the words, but 'lose value' makes me stop and ask: against the dollar, or to prices at the bazaar, and does it mean on paper or money I actually lost.
screens.why3: Rupees lose value every month here, so I would just say yes without thinking of a real time; it is a general fact, not something I did.
screens.why4: Yes and No are fine, but a gate should have no escape and this one has two: 'I'd rather not say' should not exist, and 'I can't recall one particular exchange' makes no sense for a question about value.
screens.why5: It drifted from my situation, changing leftover rupees into dollars, to whether savings lost value, and 'leftover rupees' is not how I talk; I would say my savings or extra money.
screens.why6: Short, one question, closing with 'Yes or no.', easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you change any of your rupee savings into dollars? Yes or no.

screens.why1: After the questions on my leftover rupees losing value, showing an idea for turning rupees into dollars is the obvious next step for Part 2.
screens.why2: Stablecoins, escrow and a seller paid by bank transfer or JazzCash are plain to me from Binance P2P, but the last line saying it would put the coins in my wallet 'with no jargon' is muddled and makes me read it twice.
screens.why3: I have bought dollars from local sellers by bank transfer and held USDT myself, so I can picture exactly how this would work for me.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: The how is clear, but 'with no jargon' sounds like the company's own sales line, and the belief only repeats the how instead of saying what it would do for my savings.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is long, says 'dollar stablecoins' and 'a wallet in your name' twice over, and the closing belief adds nothing new to hold on to.
screens.instead: Imagine Karsa, an app to buy dollar stablecoins from a verified local seller. You pick an amount, pay the seller by bank transfer or mobile wallet, and the app holds the coins until your payment clears, then puts them in a wallet in your name. The people building it believe this would let you keep your savings in dollars without haggling in chats for every trade.

screens.why1: After the Karsa card it makes sense to ask if I could pay for dollars, but 'your last exchange' was never set up; the earlier screens only asked if my rupees lost value, not about any time I changed them.
screens.why2: 'Exchange' could mean the money changer, the Binance app, or a swap I made, and 'a seller' assumes I bought from a person, so I'd have to stop and work out which exchange you mean.
screens.why3: Yes, I know this one: when I buy USDT on P2P I send the seller the rupees from my bank app, so I can answer from what I actually did.
screens.why4: The question is about one exchange, my last one, but 'Yes, most of the time' and 'Only sometimes' are about many times, so they overlap and don't fit a single occasion; a plain yes, yes with some steps, or no would match.
screens.why5: Paying 'a seller' by bank transfer brings in a person-to-person buying setup that I wasn't told about; I'd call it 'the person I bought dollars from', so the framing drifts toward the founder's idea of the deal.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and four short options plus 'you can't tell' are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you changed rupees into dollars. Could you pay the person or place you bought from by bank transfer? Yes / Yes, with some steps / No; escape: I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the card and the bank-transfer question, asking whether Karsa would have made my last rupee-to-dollar exchange go better is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: "Go better" is plain enough, but "exchange" could mean the swap itself or the whole back-and-forth chatting with the seller, so I'd read it twice to know which part you mean.
screens.why3: I remember my last swap on Binance P2P, the chats, the premium I paid, so I can judge from that.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, worse covers it, and "I can't tell" fits since I've only got the one-line card to go on.
screens.why5: The card only says "dollar stablecoins in a wallet" and doesn't say how I'd get rupees in, so the question leans on me guessing the founder's how; nothing leaks, but the idea reaches me thin.
screens.why6: One short question, four short options I can hold, one escape said last; it says well.
screens.instead: Would Karsa have made your last swap of rupees into dollars go better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking if I could pay by bank transfer and whether it would have helped, asking if I'd trust paying a stranger is the natural last worry, because that is how P2P on Binance already works for me.
screens.why2: Paying a seller I have never met is exactly how I buy dollars now, and verified seller is a word I see on Binance P2P every day, so I can answer at once.
screens.why3: I already pay strangers by bank transfer for USDT, so I know from my own deals whether I would do it.
screens.why4: The four are distinct and I can't tell fits, but Yes, if it was clearly worth it is odd here because worth it is not my worry with a stranger, being cheated or having my account frozen is, so an option like Yes, if my money was held safe until the dollars came is missing.
screens.why5: The card names Karsa and stablecoins on purpose, and the question only says what I would do, without bringing in any of the company's own terms for me.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, and the four options are easy to keep in mind when heard.
screens.instead: To use Karsa, you'd pay a verified seller you have never met. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Yes, if my money was held until the dollars came · Probably not · No · I can't tell
